searchText: It's all a matter of curiosity. Definitely learning languages such as Go or Rust can help a lot with understanding how some of algorithms in blockchain nodes are implemented. For Ethereum, a good idea is to try running an eth1 or eth2 node yourself and asking questions about the different components that power them. For example: "how does the chain sync?" or how is data stored, how does the p2p networking work, what are the APIs available to me, etc. Then, a place to start is by looking for good first issues in popular open source projects such as go-ethereum or others and communicating with the developers on what you can help with And don't forget to have fun (: Please check this: https://github.com/ethereum-cdap/cohort-one/blob/master/development-updates.md haha yea. If anyone planning to stick long term this is essential. 💯 Similar questions esp around "who is a core dev" were also asked to <@552133098075193354> on the bankless "layer zero" podcast and is well worth a listen! https://pca.st/yjxj6726 Here's something by Hudson Jameson, ex Ethereum Core Dev https://hudsonjameson.com/2020-06-22-what-is-an-ethereum-core-developer/ What amazing resources and context provided to this question 👏 👏 We should make an official ethereum blog post maybe? 👀 To clarify, this was <@552133098075193354>, not @ timfish.eth, I just finished listening to it yesterday and it was awesome 🙂 Sorry, blame my fat fingers. thank you all! <@!840137734768689163> <@!834543635587924028> <@!311971895828283393> https://twitter.com/0xtrent/status/1468259809292169227?t=Kc5I1Fxbx5cRAk7qGdUN5w&s=19 <@420951281910284289> You mind telling more about this 👀 still working on it, hopefully something public soon!
